extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, aesthetics, and art theory
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for judging beauty and artistic production: how taste, genius, purposiveness, and moral feeling bear on aesthetic evaluation and the method (or lack thereof) for teaching/producing beautiful art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as the faculty of aesthetical Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is the faculty of aesthetical Ideas; in the products of genius it is the nature of the subject (not premeditated purpose or rule) that gives the rule to the art. The beautiful must not be judged by concepts, but by the purposive attuning of the Imagination to agreement with the faculty of concepts in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art that is genuinely beautiful issues from gifted originality (genius) rather than from adherence to prescriptive rules. Aesthetic production that is merely rule-based or premeditated is an anti-pattern: it risks stifling genius and producing workmanship that may be 'correct' but not genuinely beautiful. Teaching should avoid prescribing fixed formulas that replace the free play of imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetical Ideas are inexponible; rational Ideas are indemonstrable
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetical Idea is an inexponible representation of the Imagination (an intuition for which an adequate concept can never be found); a rational Idea is an indemonstrable concept of Reason (a concept for which an adequate intuition can never be given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain aesthetic or rational standpoints cannot be fully expressed or demonstrated by concepts or empirical intuition; evaluation must allow for ideas that exceed complete conceptual exposition. Anti-pattern: demanding full demonstrability or a complete conceptual account for what is essentially symbolical or inexponible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of taste: empiricism versus rationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste can be grounded empirically (beauty equated with the pleasant) or placed on a priori grounds (rationalism), though these a priori grounds cannot be comprehended in definite concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing beauty merely to pleasures of sense (empiricism) or conflating aesthetic judgement with determinate moral or cognitive 'good' (rationalism in the sense of definite concepts). A legitimate aesthetic judgement appeals to a priori grounds of satisfaction that are not expressible as determinate concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism vs Idealism of purposiveness (idealism as the correct principle of taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between aesthetic realism (purposiveness as an objective purpose in nature or art) and idealism (purposive harmony as a subjective feature of our judgement). For the judgement of taste the principle must be idealism: purposiveness is placed in the subject's representation, not as an objective property of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating beauty, do not assume that nature or the artwork literally intends our satisfaction. The correct move is to locate purposiveness in the harmonious play of faculties in the subject. Anti-pattern: explaining beauty by alleging actual purposive design in nature/art (overreaching realism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four characteristic marks of a judgement of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste (what makes something 'beautiful') is characterized by: (1) it pleases immediately (without discursive cognition), (2) it pleases apart from any interest (disinterested pleasure), (3) it represents the freedom of the Imagination as harmonious with the conformity to law of the Understanding, and (4) its subjective principle is represented as universal (it lays claim to validity for every rational subject) though not through a universal concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four tests when assessing whether an object is beautiful: immediate pleasure, disinterestedness, free play/harmony of faculties, and a claim to communicable universality. Anti-patterns: pleasure tied to personal interest or desire, pleasure requiring a determinate concept, or evaluating beauty purely on empirical grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as the symbol of morality
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful serves as a symbol of the morally good: it yields a feeling of ennoblement that aligns higher cognitive faculties with moral ideas, and thus gives pleasure that appears valid for mankind in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how an aesthetic object can evoke a moral-like elevation or resonance; part of taste's claim to universality is its link to moral feeling. However, do not conflate 'beauty' with moral goodness as identical—beauty functions symbolically rather than constitutively as moral proof. Anti-pattern: treating an object's beauty as direct evidence of its moral worth without acknowledging symbolic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Taste: 'manner' not 'method' (no science of the beautiful)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no systematic science (methodus) of the beautiful; only a manner (modus). The master must show the pupil what to do and how, and universal rules serve primarily as reminders, not prescriptions; overreliance on rules stifles genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogy in art should focus on demonstration, cultivation of faculties, critical engagement, and exposure to exemplary works rather than rigid rule-instruction. Anti-pattern: rigid rulebooks or formulaic teaching that prioritizes imitation over critical development of imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaedeutic to taste: humaniora and cultivation of moral feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper preparation for taste lies in the culture of the mental powers by means of humaniora—development of sympathy and the faculty for universal communication of inner feelings—and in the cultivation of moral Ideas and moral feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training for sound aesthetic judgement should include broad humanistic education and moral cultivation; these foster the sympathetic, communicative sensibility that underpins taste. Anti-pattern: expecting reliable taste solely from technical instruction or isolated aesthetic exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement is regulative, not constitutive
rubrics_metrics.description: The teleological judgement (judging nature/art by purposes) is rightly used problematically and regulatively to bring phenomena under principles of observation where mechanical causality does not suffice; it should not be turned into a constitutive principle that introduces a new kind of objective causality (actual purposes) into nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use purposive reasoning as an explanatory heuristic or organising principle in inquiry, not as a metaphysical claim that nature literally acts with purposes. Anti-pattern: treating teleology as a literal scientific explanation where mechanical causality is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of objective purposiveness: formal vs material
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective purposiveness can be merely formal (e.g., geometrical figures whose form is objectively useful for many problems—an intellectual purposiveness) as distinct from material purposiveness; the evaluative focus should register whether purposiveness is an intellectual suitability or a material/empirical end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the purposiveness of a form (in nature, science, or art), clarify whether its purposiveness is formal (suitable for intellectual ends, problem-solving) or material (serving particular empirical ends). Example: geometrical constructions show formal, objective purposiveness. Anti-pattern: conflating different senses of 'purpose' in critique.
